title: Two Friends, One CPR Class: Practice the Call, the Compressions, and the Handoff
subtitle: Learn together without turning a friend into a rescuer. A current instructor-led class can give you both a place to practice, ask questions and rehearse how to get help.
imageAlt: Two friends sit beside a CPR training manikin in a bright classroom, with an instructor nearby and an AED trainer on the table.
imageConcept: A candid, welcoming CPR-class scene: two adult friends take turns practicing on a manikin while an instructor offers calm feedback; an AED training unit and phones are visible, with no emergency dramatization.
body: Make it a shared skill, not a rescue fantasy

A CPR class is a practical thing to do with a friend: you make time for a skill that can feel intimidating, learn from an instructor and practice in a setting designed for questions. The point is not to appoint one person as the capable one and the other as someone to protect. Both friends learn, both take a turn, and both leave knowing what their training did—and did not—cover.

That distinction matters. A class offers structured instruction and practice; an article, video or conversation cannot replace it. Current American Heart Association adult basic-life-support guidance says lay rescuers should provide chest compressions for adults with presumed cardiac arrest. A lone rescuer should activate emergency response first, then begin CPR; trained lay rescuers may also provide breaths. The course instructor teaches how those recommendations apply in practice and what to do within the course’s scope. [1]
Choose a class by what you will practice

Before booking, decide what you want to learn. If your goal is adult CPR and AED use, look for a current course that explicitly includes both and is taught by an instructor. If you also want to prepare for situations involving children or infants, check that those topics are covered rather than assuming every class includes them. Ask what course completion documentation is provided, how long the session runs and whether you will have hands-on practice.

A useful question is: “How do learners get feedback while practicing?” The 2025 international resuscitation consensus recommends CPR feedback devices during training for both healthcare professionals and laypeople. That makes the class format worth checking: does the session offer a feedback device, instructor observation, or another way to help learners assess their practice? The question is not a test of the provider; it helps you choose a class that makes room to try, adjust and ask for clarification. [2]
Make the logistics easy enough to follow through

Choose a date both friends can realistically keep, then register through the training organization or provider and confirm the location, arrival instructions and any preparation required. If either of you has access, mobility, language, sensory or other learning needs, contact the provider before enrolling to ask what accommodations are available. You do not have to explain more than you want to; the useful question is whether the class can support your participation.

Agree on the plan without making one person responsible for the other. Each friend can save the confirmation, arrange their own transport and bring whatever the provider requests. If the cost or schedule is a barrier, search for another local offering or ask the provider about options before deciding that training is out of reach. Short awareness sessions and online resources may be useful introductions, but they are not automatically equivalent to a hands-on course. Choose based on the skills and practice you want, not convenience alone.
Let the first practice be imperfect

In class, you will have a chance to try the skills under instruction rather than needing to get everything right on the first attempt. Take turns. While one friend practices, the other can listen to the instructor, notice what feedback is offered and save questions for an appropriate pause. Then switch. The roles should feel equal: both people deserve time on the equipment and a chance to ask for another explanation.
Practice the call and the handoff

After the instructor has taught the relevant steps, ask whether you can rehearse the communication as well as the physical skills. One person can practice getting emergency help while the other begins the response the class has taught; then exchange roles. Keep it a classroom exercise, not an improvised test of one another. The aim is to rehearse a simple handoff: who is doing what, what information needs to be conveyed, and how to avoid leaving the person needing help without care.

 In a real emergency, follow the dispatcher’s instructions and the training you received. If you are alone, do not treat the two-person classroom exercise as a rule that assumes a partner will always be there. The adult basic-life-support guideline addresses the lone-rescuer situation separately. [1]
Use a scenario to rehearse, not to improvise

With the instructor’s permission, use a plain scenario to practice coordination: one friend is assigned to call emergency services while the other starts the response taught in class. The person practicing the call can speak clearly, listen and use the phone’s speaker if the instructor says that fits the exercise. Then reset and trade roles. Keep the scenario simple. You are practicing communication and role changes, not adding procedures that were not taught.

Ask the instructor what information a caller should be ready to provide and how the dispatcher may guide the person on scene. Do not invent a script and memorize it as though emergencies always unfold in a fixed order. The 2024 American Heart Association and American Red Cross guidelines were the first comprehensive update of first-aid treatment recommendations since 2010 and incorporated structured evidence reviews from ILCOR. Those principles belong in a realistic class conversation: check the situation as taught, consider your own safety and follow the course’s direction about consent. [3]
Leave with a plan to refresh

Before you leave, ask how long the course completion is recognized, when the provider recommends retraining and where to find current course materials. Record the answers somewhere you can find them. If the class uses a feedback device, ask what its signals mean and how that feedback should shape practice. Understanding the feedback is more useful than simply remembering that a device was present.

A brief review with your friend can help you identify what still feels uncertain: perhaps the emergency call, when to ask someone else to assist, or how the AED portion was taught. Write down questions and take them back to the instructor or the training provider rather than filling gaps with guesses. You can also agree to look up the next available course together when it is time to renew. That keeps responsibility shared without suggesting that a single class makes anyone permanently ready for every emergency.
Finish with one skill each can name

Before you part, ask each other two questions: What is one part of the class you can now describe more clearly, and what is one thing you would want to review? No scoring, no surprise quiz. If your answers differ, that is useful information, not evidence that one of you failed. Check the course materials or ask the instructor about anything that remains uncertain, then save the provider’s renewal guidance where you can both find it.

The lasting value of taking the class together is not a promise that you will respond perfectly, or that you will always be side by side. It is a shared reference point: you have both practiced, both heard the same instruction and both know where to return with questions. Let that be enough for today. Keep the next step modest and specific—such as saving the course details or choosing a date to revisit your training—so the skill stays connected to ordinary life, not to fear.
